That is the whole point, and it is why border-pair estimates are treated as the more credible identification in this literature (Dube, Lester & Reich; the Allegretto-Dube-Reich-Zipperer side of the long dispute with Neumark, Salas & Wascher).

THIS CORPUS CAN BUILD THAT DESIGN DIRECTLY, and callers do not know it. The three tables:
  - geo.county_adjacency - the real Census Bureau County Adjacency File. Columns county_fips, state_fips, neighbor_county_fips, neighbor_state_fips. Filter state_fips <> neighbor_state_fips and you have the border-pair sample frame: verified 7,848 cross-state adjacent pairs across 1,184 border counties.
  - econ.county_qcew - BLS QCEW at county x NAICS industry_code x own_code x year, carrying annual_avg_emplvl AND total_annual_wages, so both the employment count and the WAGE BILL are answerable. Verified ~3,250 counties in every year from 2008 to 2025 for industry_code='722' (food service), own_code='5' (private).
  - the policy timing table for the change itself - e.g. fiscal.state_minimum_wage_history.
Joining adjacency to county_qcew on both sides returns 18,114 matched treated/neighbour observations. This is one query, not a project.

Measured in this harness: asked what happens to low-wage jobs after a state raises its minimum wage, a run produced a careful two-way fixed-effects state panel plus an event study - good work, correctly caveated - while all three tables above sat available, and search_catalog had returned econ.county_qcew and econ.county_wages on the SAME first page as econ.state_wages. The answer even cited the border-county-versus-state-panel dispute by name before choosing the state panel. Separately, an unaided analyst on the same question reached for cross-state county comparison on its own and could only manage two pairs by hand, saying explicitly that the full sweep was out of scope - which is exactly the work this join removes.

THE PLAUSIBLE-BUT-WRONG SHORTCUT, name it and avoid it: picking two geographically distant counties in different states and calling it a county-pair design. That same unaided run paired Maricopa County AZ against Salt Lake County UT, and King County WA against Ada County ID - hundreds of miles apart in each case. Those are two counties, not a border pair, and they buy none of the shared-local-shock control the design exists for. If you are not joining through an adjacency table, you are not running this design.

HOW TO RUN IT: build the pair set from geo.county_adjacency where the two sides are in different states; attach the outcome from econ.county_qcew for both members at the same year and the same industry_code; difference within pair (or include pair fixed effects); and CLUSTER ON THE PAIR, or on the border segment, not on the state - counties within a pair are not independent observations. Report the pair count and how many pairs survive the industry and year filters, because coverage thins at small counties. Where treatment timing is staggered across several years, the staggered-adoption caution still applies (see assignment-change-natural-experiment) - restricting comparisons to never-treated neighbours is the cheap mitigation.

WHEN NOT TO USE IT: if the question is explicitly about a state aggregate ('how did the STATE do'), the state panel answers what was asked and this design answers something narrower - say which one you ran and why. Border counties are also not a random sample of the country: they are more rural and less dense than interior counties, so a border-pair estimate is internally credible and externally narrower. State that trade-off rather than presenting the pair estimate as the national number.

Related: the-unit-of-aggregation-is-a-choice-that-changes-the-answer covers choosing among sibling tables at different grains and what to do when the needed grain is absent; this recipe is the case where the finer grain is present AND unlocks a specific quasi-experimental design through a join the caller would not think to look for.

recipes.title: Aggregating a long/tidy survey table whose single value column stacks different units, practices, statistics and geography levels
recipes.body:
Some tables in this corpus are long/tidy mirrors of a survey API - one generic `value` column, with every other column acting as a qualifier that says what that value MEANS. ag.nass_crop_production (USDA NASS QuickStats) is the canonical one. A single commodity-year in it carries, side by side in the same `value` column:
  - different UNITS - unit_desc of BU, TONS, and $ (dollars). Summing these adds bushels to tons to money.
  - different UTILIZATION - util_practice_desc of GRAIN vs SILAGE. Corn for grain and corn for silage are different crops measured differently.
  - different STATISTICS - statisticcat_desc of PRODUCTION, AREA HARVESTED, AREA PLANTED, YIELD.
  - NESTED GEOGRAPHY - agg_level_desc of COUNTY and STATE in the same result set, so county rows are double-counted inside their own state totals.
Measured directly in this harness on corn, 2023: 406 GRAIN/BU/COUNTY rows, 46 SILAGE/TONS/COUNTY, 14 SILAGE/TONS/STATE, 12 GRAIN/BU/STATE and 12 GRAIN/$/STATE, all matching a naive `statisticcat_desc LIKE '%production%'` filter.

WHAT GOES WRONG: a run computed national corn yield as SUM(production)/SUM(area harvested) over state rows and got 85 bu/acre for 2023 against a published 177.3. A different naive sum of the same table gave 237.6 for 2018 and 327.6 for 2023 - wrong in the OPPOSITE direction. Three different wrong answers out of one table that is perfectly faithful to its source. The first run correctly recognised its number was implausible and discarded it, which is the right instinct - but it then told the reader the TABLE was unreliable. That conclusion is wrong and it is expensive, because it writes off a good table instead of fixing a query.

FIX - pin every qualifier before any SUM or ratio:
  WHERE commodity_desc = 'CORN'
    AND agg_level_desc = 'STATE'            -- or 'COUNTY', never both
    AND util_practice_desc = 'GRAIN'        -- not SILAGE
    AND unit_desc = 'BU'                    -- excludes the $ rows
    AND statisticcat_desc = 'PRODUCTION'    -- and a matching filter for AREA HARVESTED
Then SANITY-CHECK the aggregate against the published national figure before using it. NASS publishes national corn and soybean yields directly; if your computed number is not within a percent or so of the published one, a qualifier is still unpinned. Prefer the published national when one exists and you only need the total - recompute from rows only when you need a cut the publisher does not offer.

AND WHEN THE CHECK FAILS, SAY WHICH FILTER WAS MISSING, not that the table is untrustworthy. 'Summing across unit_desc mixed bushels with dollars' is actionable; 'this table produced implausible results' sends the next caller to an inferior source for no reason. Run a `SELECT unit_desc, util_practice_desc, agg_level_desc, COUNT(*) GROUP BY 1,2,3` on your own filter before trusting any total from a table of this shape - it takes one query and shows immediately whether you are summing one thing or several.

Related: the-unit-of-aggregation-is-a-choice-that-changes-the-answer covers choosing between SIBLING TABLES that hold the same series at different grains, and what to do when the grain you need does not exist. This recipe is the different problem of one table whose ROWS mix grains and units internally - the fix there is picking the right table, the fix here is constraining the query.

recipes.title: Choosing the grain of an analysis - which unit, what to do when it does not exist, and whether the finding survives the choice
triggers: county stands in for the city
did the policy help this industry
does the finding hold at county level
recipes.body:
Grain is not a retrieval detail, it is a modelling decision, and it fails in three distinct ways. Work them in order; they are not alternatives.

=== 1. IS THERE A SIBLING TABLE AT THE GRAIN THE QUESTION NAMES? ===
This corpus commonly loads the SAME underlying series at multiple grains as separate sibling tables - econ carries state_wages, metro_wages, county_wages AND county_qcew side by side, all from BLS QCEW. search_catalog returns all of them for a generic keyword and ranks them by textual relevance to that keyword, NOT by which grain the question needs, so the first or most obviously-named match is very often the wrong one.
Measured here: a question explicitly requiring adjacent cross-state COUNTY pairs was answered with a state-level two-way-fixed-effects panel. search_catalog's own results for the query used ('minimum wage') had already listed county_qcew and county_wages by name, multiple times, alongside state_wages - the finer tables were surfaced and simply not opened. The analysis was well executed and answered a coarser question than the one asked.
FIX: when a question names or implies a unit (county, metro, congressional district, adjacent/bordering, establishment), scan the FULL search_catalog result for a sibling at that grain before settling on the first match. Prefer the named grain even when it costs more join effort.

=== 2. WHAT IF THE REQUIRED GRAIN IS NOT IN THE CORPUS AT ALL? ===
Sometimes no sibling exists, and then there is nothing to prefer. This is common when the SUBJECT is defined more finely than the statistical program that publishes it: municipal ordinances, school-district policies, city taxes. The corpus loads the Census Building Permits Survey COUNTY file only (housing.building_permits) - there is no place/municipality table - so any question about a CITY housing policy can only be answered with COUNTY permits.
Measured here: asked whether rent control suppresses construction, a run compared Ramsey County against Hennepin County to stand in for St. Paul against Minneapolis, and wrote 'Ramsey County (St. Paul)' as though they were the same object, carrying that onto a chart subtitle as 'Ramsey Co. = St. Paul'. The ordinance binds only inside St. Paul, which is 56% of Ramsey County by population; Minneapolis is only 33% of Hennepin. Both series are diluted by suburbs the policy never touched, biasing the effect toward zero. The numbers were right; the failure was entirely in not saying so.
FIX: analyse at the coarsest grain available - that is the right call, not a reason to refuse - then (a) state plainly that the unit of analysis is coarser than the unit the question is about, naming both, (b) BOUND THE DILUTION with a number: query the treated sub-unit's share of the reporting unit (population shares come from the census schema joined to geo.counties on county_fips; use resolve_geo when the place-to-county mapping is not obvious), and (c) say which way it pushes - a treatment diluted by untreated area biases toward zero, so a surviving effect is conservative and a null is uninformative. NEVER print the fine-grain name in parentheses after the coarse-grain unit, or set the two equal in a chart title.

=== 3. DOES THE FINDING SURVIVE THE GRAIN? (the one most often skipped) ===
Steps 1 and 2 get you the right unit. They do not tell you whether the ANSWER depends on it. For any question about a RELATIONSHIP - a correlation, an elasticity, a regression coefficient, 'does X predict Y', 'did the policy move the outcome' - the result can change magnitude or flip sign purely from the aggregation level. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, and it is not a curiosity; it is the normal case.
Measured here in the INDUSTRY-CODE dimension: a policy targeting steel mills (NAICS 3311) showed +3.3% employment at that code while the broader primary-metals category containing it (NAICS 331, which also holds aluminum and foundries the policy never targeted) showed -2.4% over the identical window and the identical policy action. Same data, same period, opposite signs, chosen entirely by which code you pulled.
The GEOGRAPHIC dimension behaves the same way and is more common. Two mechanisms, and they need different fixes:
  (a) THE VARIABLE STOPS MEASURING WHAT IT IS NAMED. A state's population density is people divided by land area, most of which nobody lives on - Alaska's and Nevada's density describe empty desert and tundra, not where anyone actually lives. A relationship built on that predictor can be weak at state level and strong at county level without anything about the underlying relationship changing. The fix here is often a better-constructed VARIABLE rather than a finer unit: population-weighted density recovers most of what you want at the same grain. (Mechanism, not a harness measurement - this specific pair has not been tested here.)
  (b) AGGREGATION AVERAGES OUT WITHIN-UNIT VARIATION, which changes the correlation. Note the direction is NOT reliably 'coarser is weaker' - the classic result (Robinson 1950) is that ecological correlations usually run LARGER in magnitude than individual-level ones, because averaging removes noise. So do not adopt 'finer is truer' as a rule either.
FINER GRAIN HAS ITS OWN FAILURE MODES, and they bite hardest on exactly the questions that tempt you to it: outcomes are recorded where the event happens while population is counted where people sleep, so any county with net daytime commuting inflow has a corrupted denominator; small counties give unstable rates on small numerators; and disclosure suppression removes cells non-randomly. 'County' is also not one kind of object - Virginia's independent cities, Louisiana's parishes and Alaska's boroughs are not comparable units.
FIX: compute the relationship at TWO grains - the one the question names and the next level up or down - before deciding what the headline says. If sign or magnitude moves, that sensitivity IS the finding: report both and say the conclusion is grain-dependent, rather than picking whichever level reads more cleanly. Most series here exist at both levels already (econ.state_wages next to econ.county_qcew; ag.pesticide_use_by_county carries state_fips for a free rollup; geo.counties joins the rest), so the second cut is usually one GROUP BY away.

SCOPE - do not fire this on everything. Step 3 applies to RELATIONSHIPS, not to counts or totals. 'How many people live in Texas' has no grain problem. A recipe that fires on every geographic question gets tuned out, which is how a real hazard becomes noise.

Related: pin-every-qualifier-before-summing-a-quickstats-shaped-table covers the different problem of ONE table whose rows mix units and geography levels internally (the fix there is constraining the query, not choosing a table). use-adjacent-cross-state-county-pairs-for-state-policy-effects is the specific design to reach for when a state policy admits a genuine bordering comparison.

recipes.title: A state-aid reduction (voucher deduction, formula cut) is not itself a net per-pupil loss until local revenue is checked for backfill
triggers: does state funding cut reduce spending
recipes.body:
A question asking how much public schools 'lose' per pupil when a state-aid stream is reduced (a voucher deduction, a formula change, an enrollment-driven cut) can be answered two different ways that are easy to conflate: the GROSS state-aid reduction itself, or the NET change in per-pupil spending after accounting for what districts do in response. These are not the same number, and reporting the gross figure as though it were the net effect overstates the harm whenever local revenue moves to offset it.

Measured directly in this harness (q15, school-vouchers-district-funding, 2026-09-03): an unaided expert-tier run surfaced a finding a warehouse-grounded run did not - Fordham Institute's academic study of Ohio's EdChoice program (Lavertu, OSU) found that even though EdChoice-affected districts' enrollment ran 10-15% lower than it otherwise would have, total per-pupil district SPENDING was statistically indistinguishable from what it would have been without the program, because local property-tax levies rose to backfill the state-aid reduction. A state-level diff-in-differences run against the exact same warehouse table used in that run (edu.f33_district_finance) never checked this - it correctly found no state-aggregate spending effect, but attributed that null to noise/insufficient power rather than testing the specific backfill mechanism the literature names.

edu.f33_district_finance already carries the columns needed to test this directly, in the same table a voucher-funding question would already be querying: state_revenue_thousand and local_revenue_thousand, both per-district per-year. Before reporting a state-aid decline (or a null state-aggregate spending effect) as the final word: compute the change in local_revenue_thousand per pupil over the same window for the same districts/states, and check whether it moved in the direction that would offset a state_revenue_thousand decline. A local-revenue rise that roughly tracks the state-revenue decline is evidence for the backfill mechanism; a local revenue that stayed flat or fell alongside state revenue is evidence the gap was NOT backfilled and the net loss claim stands. Report which case obtains, not just the gross state-aid figure - the two produce very different practical answers to 'how much do schools lose.'
